Abstract.

In this paper we explore conditions for a curve in a smooth projective surface to have a free product of cyclic groups as the fundamental group of its complement. It is known that if the surface is ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}, then such curves must be of fiber type, i.e. a finite union of fibers of an admissible map onto a complex curve. In this setting, we exhibit an infinite family of Zariski pairs of fiber-type curves, that is, pairs of plane projective fiber-type curves whose tubular neighborhoods are homeomorphic, but whose embeddings in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} are not. This includes a Zariski pair of curves in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with only nodes as singularities (and the same singularities at infinity) whose complements have non-isomorphic fundamental groups, one of them being free. Our examples show that the position of nodes also affects the topology of the embedding of projective curves. Twisted Alexander polynomials with respect to finite SU⁡(2)\SU(2) representations show to be useful for this purpose, since all their abelian invariants are the same for both fundamental groups.

32S25, 32S55, 32S05, 32S20, 57K31

1. Introduction

In a series of recent papers by different authors ([MR4349417, Catanese-Fibred, Arapura-toward, ji-Eva-orbifold]) there is a growing interest in studying the connection between the geometric properties of a smooth connected complex quasi-projective surface UU and its fundamental group. This paper continues [ji-Eva-orbifold], which deals with the case where π1​(U)\pi_{1}(U) is a free product of cyclic groups.

One of the main results by the authors in this direction is [ji-Eva-orbifold, Theorem 1.3], which gives geometric necessary conditions for a curve inside of a smooth projective surface to have a free product of cyclic groups as the fundamental group of its complement. The flavor of this result can be summarized as follows: if XX is a smooth connected complex projective surface and D⊂XD\subset X is a curve such that π1​(X∖D)\pi_{1}(X\setminus D) is a free product of cyclic groups, then there exists a smooth projective curve SS and an admissible (see Definition 2.1) map F:X∖ℬ→SF:X\setminus\mathcal{B}\to S inducing an isomorphism π1​(X∖D)→π1orb​(S)\pi_{1}(X\setminus D)\to\pi^{\orb}_{1}(S), where ℬ\mathcal{B} is a finite set of points in DD and π1orb​(S)\pi^{\orb}_{1}(S) is the orbifold fundamental group for some orbifold structure on SS induced by the multiplicity of the fibers of F|X∖DF_{|X\setminus D}. Moreover, DD is the closure of a finite union of fibers of FF and of special null-homology horizontal components. In the particular case where X=ℙ2X=\mathbb{P}^{2}, the curve DD is the closure of a finite union of fibers of FF, which we refer to as a fiber-type curve. See Theorem 2.14 in section 2.3 for the precise statement when X=ℙ2X=\mathbb{P}^{2}.

The question of whether or not, or to what extent, this is a sufficient condition arises. For instance, if X=ℙ2X=\mathbb{P}^{2}, U:=X∖DU:=X\setminus D, and DD contains only generic fibers of an admissible map (satisfying Condition 2.3 in section 2.1), then π1​(U)\pi_{1}(U) is a free product of cyclic groups (see [ji-Eva-orbifold, Theorem 1.2]). However on the other end, if DD contains all atypical fibers of an admissible map, then π1​(U)\pi_{1}(U) tends to not be a free product of cyclic groups, but rather a semidirect product of the fundamental groups of two smooth quasi-projective curves [ji-Eva-orbifold, Lemma 2.18, Corollary 2.19]. Thus, it is natural to ask if it is possible to formulate sufficient conditions for the fundamental group of a curve complement to be a free product of cyclic groups in terms of the topology of the fibers contained in DD in the case when some of these fibers contain only mild singularities (for example nodes).

In section 3, we describe this problem in more precise terms. Given an admissible map F:X∖ℬ→SF:X\setminus\mathcal{B}\to S and BF⊂SB_{F}\subset S the set of atypical values of FF, we define 𝒯F⊂𝒫⁡(BF){\mathcal{T}}_{F}\subset\mathcal{P}(B_{F}) the family of subsets TT of BFB_{F} such that F∗F_{*} induces an isomorphism of fundamental groups when restricted to X∖F−1​(T)X\setminus F^{-1}(T). The set of all maximal elements of 𝒯F{\mathcal{T}}_{F} with the inclusion order is called the threshold of atypical values. If X=ℙ2X=\mathbb{P}^{2}, this set 𝒯F{\mathcal{T}}_{F} completely describes the remarkable phenomenon of π1​(X∖D)\pi_{1}(X\setminus D) being a free product of cyclic groups for curves DD which are the closure of two or more fibers of FF (see Proposition 3.6). A good understanding of the threshold set of atypical values can provide a source of Zariski pairs of fiber-type curves, where the fundamental group of one of them is a free product of cyclic groups.

The main result of this paper is shown in section 4 where we explore whether or not the “free product of cyclic groups” condition for π1​(X∖D)\pi_{1}(X\setminus D) could be determined by any topological information provided by the atypical fibers of FF which lie in DD. To answer this question in the negative, we give in section 4.1 a special example of a Zariski pair of curves, both of which consist of two homeomorphic fibers in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} of the same polynomial map, plus the line at infinity. A Zariski pair (see [Artal-couples]) refers to two algebraic curves C1,C2⊂ℙ2C_{1},C_{2}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} with homeomorphic regular neighborhoods, but non-homeomorphic embeddings, that is, (ℙ2,C1)≇(ℙ2,C2)(\mathbb{P}^{2},C_{1})\not\cong(\mathbb{P}^{2},C_{2}). In particular, both curves have the same combinatorial type (see the discussion after Definition 2 in [Artal-ji-Tokunaga-survey-zariski]) which includes the same degree and the same local types of singularities. Analogously, if D1,D2⊂ℂ2D_{1},D_{2}\subset\mathbb{C}^{2} are two affine curves and one identifies ℂ2≡ℙ2∖L∞\mathbb{C}^{2}\equiv\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus L_{\infty} where L∞L_{\infty} denotes the line at infinity, then the curves D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} form an affine Zariski pair if D1∪L∞D_{1}\cup L_{\infty} and D2∪L∞D_{2}\cup L_{\infty} form a Zariski pair in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}.

The example can be described as follows: consider the family of polynomials fλ​(x,y)=x6+y6+6​x​y−λf_{\lambda}(x,y)=x^{6}+y^{6}+6xy-\lambda. One can construct two curves D1={f4⋅f−4=0}⊂ℂ2D_{1}=\{f_{4}\cdot f_{-4}=0\}\subset\mathbb{C}^{2} and D2={f4⋅f4​i=0}⊂ℂ2D_{2}=\{f_{4}\cdot f_{4i}=0\}\subset\mathbb{C}^{2}. Note that each DiD_{i} is a union of two disjoint irreducible nodal affine sextics with six nodes each. One obtains the following in Theorem 4.1.

Theorem 1.1.

The affine nodal curves D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} form an affine Zariski pair. Moreover, π1​(ℂ2∖D1)≇π1​(ℂ2∖D2)=𝔽2\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus D_{1})\not\cong\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus D_{2})=\mathbb{F}_{2} the free group of rank 2.

This exhibits two fiber-type curves as unions of two fibers of the polynomial map f:ℂ2→ℂf:\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} defined by f⁡(x,y)=x6+y6+6​x​yf(x,y)=x^{6}+y^{6}+6xy. Each fiber is a sextic with six nodes. The main result shows that the particular choice of the two fibers given in D1D_{1} (resp. D2D_{2}) produces a non-free (resp. a free) group.

As a word of caution between the affine and projective cases, it is known that projective nodal curves have abelian fundamental groups (cf. [Fulton-Fundamental, deligne-groupe]) and hence there cannot be a Zariski pair of projective nodal curves.

One can also consider the closure of these curves in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}. This is done in section 4.2, were we prove that the union of the two sextics for both of these curves yields two projective curves of degree 1212 which also form a Zariski pair. In particular, consider Fλ​(X,Y,Z)F_{\lambda}(X,Y,Z) the homogenization of fλ​(x,y)f_{\lambda}(x,y) and the projective curves C1={F4⋅F−4=0}⊂ℙ2C_{1}=\{F_{4}\cdot F_{-4}=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} and C2={F4⋅F4​i=0}⊂ℙ2C_{2}=\{F_{4}\cdot F_{4i}=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}. We prove the following in Theorem 4.6.

Theorem 1.2.

The projective curves C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} form a Zariski pair. Moreover, π1​(ℙ2∖C2)=ℤ∗ℤ6≇π1​(ℙ2∖C1)\pi_{1}(\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus C_{2})=\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}_{6}\not\cong\pi_{1}(\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus C_{1}).

Note that other examples of Zariski pairs where there is a connection between the topology of their complement and the position of singular points (including nodes) have been exhibited before (see [Tokunaga-Geometry, Bannai-Shirane-Nodal]). However, the remarkable aspect of the present family of examples stands for the fact that the only special position of singularities is given by the nodes.

In section 4.3 we classify all possible fundamental groups of complements of fiber-type curves obtained from fibers of the rational map F:ℙ2⇢ℙ1F:\mathbb{P}^{2}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} introduced above. This completely characterizes all the (infinitely many) Zariski pairs whose irreducible components are fibers of this morphism, and such that the fundamental groups of their complements satisfy that one of them is a free product of cyclic groups (see Theorem 4.9).

Theorem 1.3.

Let F:U→ℙ1F:U\to\mathbb{P}^{1} be given by F=[x6+y6+6xyz4:z6]F=[x^{6}+y^{6}+6xyz^{4}:z^{6}], where U=ℙ2∖{[x:y:0]∣x6+y6=0}U=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\{[x:y:0]\mid x^{6}+y^{6}=0\}. Then, the following is a complete list of all Zariski pairs of curves (CA,CA′)(C_{A},C_{A^{\prime}}) such that the fundamental group of the complement of CAC_{A} in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} is a free product of cyclic groups:

π1​(ℙ2∖CA)\pi_{1}(\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus C_{A}) AA A′A^{\prime}

Finally, in section 5 we present a discussion on the (twisted) Alexander-type invariants of the affine Zariski pair. In particular, it is shown that both curve complements have the same Alexander invariants. Note that the difference between D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} is only the position of their nodes (Lemma ). The position of nodes is known not to have an effect on Alexander polynomials or characteristic varieties [Libgober-characteristic]. However, twisted Alexander polynomials with respect to unitary respresentations in SU⁡(2)\SU(2) for these groups are different. To our knowledge, this is the first example in the literature of a Zariski pair of curves whose complements have the same characteristic varieties and whose fundamental groups have different twisted Alexander polynomials.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Admissible maps

The following definition is found in Arapura [Arapura-geometry].

Definition 2.1.

A surjective morphism F:U→SF:U\to S from a smooth quasi-projective surface UU to a smooth projective curve SS is admissible if it admits a surjective holomorphic enlargement F^:U^→S\hat{F}:\hat{U}\to S with connected fibers, where U^\hat{U} is a smooth compactification of UU.

Remark 2.2.

Let F:U→SF:U\to S be a surjective morphism from a smooth quasi-projective surface to a smooth projective curve. Then FF is admissible if and only if FF has connected generic fibers. Indeed, if F:U→SF:U\to S is admissible and F^:U^→S\hat{F}:\hat{U}\to S is a holomorphic enlargement with connected fibers, the generic fiber of F^\hat{F} is smooth by generic smoothness on the target. Hence, the generic fiber of FF is a Zariski open subset of a smooth connected compact curve, which is connected. For the other implication, suppose that F^:U^→S\hat{F}:\hat{U}\to S is a holomorphic enlargement of FF, where U^\hat{U} is a smooth compactification of UU. Then, Stein factorization implies that F^\hat{F} factors as a map with connected fibers G:X→S′G:X\to S^{\prime} and a surjective finite morphism h:S′→Sh:S^{\prime}\to S, where S′S^{\prime} can be taken to be a smooth projective curve. Since FF has connected generic fibers, and FF also factors through hh, hh must be a branched cover of degree d=1d=1, so hh is a homeomorphism and thus F^\hat{F} has connected fibers.

Most of the maps that will appear in this paper will be dominant rational morphisms F:ℙ2⇢ℙ1F:\mathbb{P}^{2}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} such that the restriction to its maximal domain of definition is an admissible map. Any dominant rational morphism FF can be expressed by a surjective morphism F=[f:g]:U→ℙ1F=[f:g]:U\to\mathbb{P}^{1} when restricted to its maximal domain of definition UU, where f,g∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]f,g\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] are homogeneous polynomials of the same degree with no non-constant common factors, and U=ℙ2∖ℬU=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}, where ℬ\mathcal{B} is the finite set V⁡(f)∩V⁡(g)V(f)\cap V(g). In particular, most of the maps that will appear in this paper will be of the form described below:

Condition 2.3.

F=[fqp:fpq]:U→ℙ1F=[f_{q}^{p}:f_{p}^{q}]:U\to\mathbb{P}^{1} is such that

  • •

    p,q∈ℤ≥1p,q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, with gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1,

  • •

    fp,fq∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]f_{p},f_{q}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] are homogeneous polynomials of degrees pp and qq respectively, with no non-constant common factors,

  • •

    neither fpf_{p} nor fqf_{q} is a kk-th power of another polynomial in ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] for any k≥2k\geq 2,

  • •

    U=ℙ2∖ℬU=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}, where ℬ\mathcal{B} is the finite set V⁡(fp)∩V⁡(fq)∈ℙ2V(f_{p})\cap V(f_{q})\in\mathbb{P}^{2},

  • •

    The map FF has no multiple fibers outside {[0:1],[1:0]}\{[0:1],[1:0]\}.

The last point in Condition 2.3 is necessary (up to change of coordinates in ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}) for FF to be admissible, as shown in the following remark.

Remark 2.4.

Let F:U→ℙ1F:U\to\mathbb{P}^{1} be the restriction to its maximal domain of definition of a dominant rational map F:ℙ2⇢ℙ1F:\mathbb{P}^{2}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}. If F:U→ℙ1F:U\to\mathbb{P}^{1} is admissible, [ji-Libgober-mw, Proposition 2.8] implies that the number of multiple fibers of FF does not exceed 22, so, after a change of coordinates in ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, we may assume that the multiple fibers of FF lie over a subset of {[0:1],[1:0]}\{[0:1],[1:0]\}.

Remark 2.5.

Let f:ℂ2→ℂf:\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} be a non-constant polynomial map with connected generic fibers. Then, ff extends to an admissible map F:ℙ2∖ℬ=[f¯(x,y,z):zd]→ℙ1F:\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}=[\overline{f}(x,y,z):z^{d}]\to\mathbb{P}^{1}, where f¯\overline{f} is the homogenization of ff with respect to the variable zz, dd is the degree of ff, and ℬ=V⁡(f¯​(x,y,z))∩V⁡(z)\mathcal{B}=V(\overline{f}(x,y,z))\cap V(z).

It is easy to construct admissible maps satisfying Condition 2.3, as exemplified by the following result.

Lemma 2.6.

Let F=[fk​qp:fk​pq]:U=ℙ2∖(V(fk​q)∩V(fk​p))→ℙ1F=[f_{kq}^{p}:f_{kp}^{q}]:U=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus(V(f_{kq})\cap V(f_{kp}))\to\mathbb{P}^{1} such that k∈ℤ≥1k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1, and fk​q,fk​p∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]f_{kq},f_{kp}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] are irreducible homogeneous polynomials of degree k​qkq and k​pkp respectively that are not constant multiples of one another. Then, FF is an admissible map. Moreover, if k=1k=1, then FF also satisfies Condition 2.3.

Proof.

Let F^:X→ℙ1\hat{F}:X\to\mathbb{P}^{1} be a resolution of indeterminacies of the pencil F:ℙ2⇢ℙ1F:\mathbb{P}^{2}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}. In particular, XX is a smooth simply connected projective surface. Using Stein factorization and the fact that XX is simply connected, F^\hat{F} factors as H∘G^H\circ\hat{G}, where G^:X→ℙ1\hat{G}:X\to\mathbb{P}^{1} has connected fibers and H:ℙ1→ℙ1H:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1} is finite, generically d:1d:1. Our goal is to show that d=1d=1. Let G:=G^|U:U→ℙ1G:=\hat{G}_{|U}:U\to\mathbb{P}^{1}, which is an admissible map by construction.

The map HH (resp. GG) is of the form [h1(x,y):h2(x,y)][h_{1}(x,y):h_{2}(x,y)] (resp. [f(x,y,z):g(x,y,z)][f(x,y,z):g(x,y,z)], where h1,h2∈ℂ⁡[x,y]h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] (resp. f,g∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]f,g\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]) are homogeneous polynomials of the same degree with no non-constant common factors. Hence,

fk​qp=h1​(f,g),fk​pq=h2​(f,g).f_{kq}^{p}=h_{1}(f,g),\quad f_{kp}^{q}=h_{2}(f,g).

Since fk​qf_{kq} and fk​pf_{kp} are irreducible and every homogeneous polynomial in ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] decomposes as a product of linear forms, we have that there exist [a:b],[c:d]∈ℙ1[a:b],[c:d]\in\mathbb{P}^{1} and m,l∈ℤ≥1m,l\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} such that

h1(x,y)=(bx−ay)m,m∣p,h2(x,y)=(dx−cy)l,l∣q,h_{1}(x,y)=(bx-ay)^{m},\quad m\mid p,\quad h_{2}(x,y)=(dx-cy)^{l},\quad l\mid q,

and since h1h_{1} and h2h_{2} have the same degree, m=lm=l. The condition that gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1 implies that m=l=1m=l=1. Hence, HH is a change of coordinates in ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, which concludes the proof of the fact that FF is admissible. By Remark 2.4, if k=1k=1, FF also satisfies Condition 2.3, since the existence of a multiple fiber over a point not in {[0:1],[1:0]}\left\{[0:1],[1:0]\right\} would imply that FF does not have connected generic fibers. ∎

Example 2.7.

The result of Lemma 2.6 is no longer true if the irreducibility assumption is dropped. For example, if fp=xp−ypf_{p}=x^{p}-y^{p} and fq=xq+yqf_{q}=x^{q}+y^{q} and pp is odd, then [fpq:fqp]:ℙ2∖{[0:0:1]}→ℙ1[f_{p}^{q}:f_{q}^{p}]:\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\{[0:0:1]\}\to\mathbb{P}^{1} is not an admissible map, since the closure of any of its fibers is a union of lines in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} going through the point [0:0:1][0:0:1].

2.2. Orbifold fundamental groups and morphisms

Let SS be a smooth projective curve of genus gg. We may endow it with an orbifold structure by choosing φ:S→ℤ≥0\varphi:S\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} such that φ⁡(P)≠1\varphi(P)\neq 1 only for a finite number of points. Let Σ=Σ0∪Σ+⊂S\Sigma=\Sigma_{0}\cup\Sigma_{+}\subset S be the points for which φ⁡(P)=0\varphi(P)=0 if P∈Σ0P\in\Sigma_{0} and φ⁡(Q)=mQ>1\varphi(Q)=m_{Q}>1 if Q∈Σ+Q\in\Sigma_{+}. We will denote this structure by S(n+1,m¯)S_{(n+1,\bar{m})}, where n+1=#​Σ0n+1=\#\Sigma_{0}, and m¯\bar{m} is a (#​Σ+)(\#\Sigma_{+})-tuple whose entries are the corresponding mQm_{Q}’s.

As a word of caution for the following definitions, the term orbifold might be misleading: we do not need to develop any theory of orbifolds or VV-manifolds in this context, but rather use the orbifold structures to highlight the existence of multiple fibers of an admissible map. This will become clear throughout the section.

Definition 2.8 (Orbifold fundamental group of a smooth projective curve).

Let S(n+1,m¯)S_{(n+1,\bar{m})} be a smooth projective curve endowed with an orbifold structure. The orbifold fundamental group of S(n+1,m¯)S_{(n+1,\bar{m})} is defined by

π1orb​(S(n+1,m¯)):=π1​(S∖Σ)/⟨μPφ⁡(P),P∈Σ⟩,\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S_{(n+1,\bar{m})}):=\pi_{1}(S\setminus\Sigma)/\langle\mu_{P}^{\varphi(P)},P\in\Sigma\rangle,

where μP\mu_{P} is a meridian in S∖ΣS\setminus\Sigma around P∈ΣP\in\Sigma, and ⟨μPφ⁡(P),P∈Σ⟩\langle\mu_{P}^{\varphi(P)},P\in\Sigma\rangle is the normal subgroup generated by the μPφ⁡(P)\mu_{P}^{\varphi(P)}’s.

In particular, if Σ0≠∅\Sigma_{0}\neq\emptyset, (1) shows that π1orb​(S(n+1,m¯))\pi_{1}^{\textrm{orb}}(S_{(n+1,\bar{m})}) is a free product of cyclic groups as follows

π1orb​(S(n+1,m¯))≅π1​(S∖Σ0)​∗⁡(∗P∈Σ+⁡(ℤmP​ℤ))≅𝔽r∗ℤm1∗⋯∗ℤms,\pi_{1}^{\textrm{orb}}(S_{(n+1,\bar{m})})\cong\pi_{1}(S\setminus\Sigma_{0})\mathop{\scalebox{1.5}{\raisebox{-0.86108pt}{$\ast$}}}\left(\mathop{\scalebox{1.5}{\raisebox{-0.86108pt}{$\ast$}}}_{P\in\Sigma_{+}}\left(\frac{\mathbb{Z}}{m_{P}\mathbb{Z}}\right)\right)\cong\mathbb{F}_{r}*\mathbb{Z}_{m_{1}}*\dots*\mathbb{Z}_{m_{s}},

where r=2​g−1+#​Σ0=2​g+nr=2g-1+\#\Sigma_{0}=2g+n, s=#​Σ+s=\#\Sigma_{+}, and m¯=(m1,…,ms)\bar{m}=(m_{1},\dots,m_{s}). Note that any finitely generated free product of cyclic groups can be realized as an orbifold fundamental group of a smooth projective curve in this way.

Definition 2.9 (Orbifold morphism).

Let UU be a smooth algebraic variety. A dominant algebraic morphism F:U→S(n+1,m¯)F:U\to S_{(n+1,\bar{m})} defines an orbifold morphism if for all P∈SP\in S such that φ⁡(P)>0\varphi(P)>0, the divisor F∗​(P)F^{*}(P) is a φ⁡(P)\varphi(P)-multiple.

Definition 2.10 (Maximal orbifold structures).

Let F:U→S(n+1,m¯)F:U\to S_{(n+1,\bar{m})} be an orbifold morphism. The orbifold S(n+1,m¯)S_{(n+1,\bar{m})} is said to be maximal (with respect to FF) if F⁡(U)=S∖Σ0F(U)=S\setminus\Sigma_{0} and for all P∈F⁡(U)P\in F(U) the divisor F∗​(P)F^{*}(P) is not an nn-multiple for any n>φ⁡(P)n>\varphi(P).

The following result is well known (see [ACM-multiple-fibers, Prop. 1.4], for example)

Remark 2.11.

Let F:U→S(n+1,m¯)F:U\to S_{(n+1,\bar{m})} be an orbifold morphism. Then, FF induces a morphism F∗:π1​(U)→π1orb​(S(n+1,m¯)).F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U)\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S_{(n+1,\bar{m})}). Moreover, if the generic fiber of FF is connected, then F∗F_{*} is surjective.

We end this section with important notational conventions that will be used throughout the rest of the paper:

  • •

    Whenever we refer to a dominant algebraic morphism F:U→SF:U\to S as an orbifold morphism, we will assume that SS is endowed with the orbifold structure that turns FF into an orbifold morphism in such a way that the orbifold structure is maximal.

  • •

    The only orbifold structures that will appear are the maximal ones.

  • •

    In particular, if F:U→SF:U\to S is surjective and B⊂SB\subset S, the notation F∗:π1​(U∖F−1​(B))→π1orb​(S∖B)F_{*}:\pi_{1}\left(U\setminus F^{-1}(B)\right)\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus B) will refer to the morphism endowed by F|U∖F−1(B):U∖F−1(B)→SF_{|U\setminus F^{-1}(B)}:U\setminus F^{-1}(B)\to S on (orbifold) fundamental groups, where SS is endowed with the maximal orbifold structure with respect to F|U∖F−1(B)F_{|U\setminus F^{-1}(B)} (which has Σ0=B\Sigma_{0}=B).

2.3. Fiber-type curves

Definition 2.12 (Fiber-type curve).

Let XX be a smooth projective surface, and let CC be a curve in XX. We say that a CC is a fiber-type curve if, for some complement of a finite number of points in XX called UU, there exists an admissible map F:U→SF:U\to S to a smooth projective curve SS such that CC is the closure in XX of a finite number of fibers of FF.

Remark 2.13.

Let f:ℂ2→ℂf:\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C} be a non-constant polynomial map with connected generic fibers. We will also refer to the union CC of a finite number of fibers of ff as an affine fiber-type curve. Indeed, both points of view agree if we want to study the topology of their complements: ff extends to an admissible map F:ℙ2∖ℬ=[f¯(x,y,z):zd]→ℙ1F:\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}=[\overline{f}(x,y,z):z^{d}]\to\mathbb{P}^{1} as in Remark 2.5. The complement in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} of the union of C¯\overline{C} and the line at infinity (which is the closure in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} of the fiber of FF over [1:0][1:0]) coincides with ℂ2∖C\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus C.

As mentioned in the introduction, the curves in a smooth projective surface XX whose complements have a fundamental group which is a free product of cyclic groups are (essentially) fiber-type curves (with perhaps some extra null-homotopic irreducible components). In fact, if X=ℙ2X=\mathbb{P}^{2}, the curves must actually be fiber-type curves, as exemplified by the following result:

Theorem 2.14 (Main Theorem for curves in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} [ji-Eva-orbifold, Cor. 3.14]).

Let DD be a curve in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}. Suppose that π1​(ℙ2∖D)\pi_{1}(\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus D) is a free product of cyclic groups. Then, there exists r≥0r\geq 0 and m1≥m2≥1m_{1}\geq m_{2}\geq 1 with gcd⁡(m1,m2)=1\gcd(m_{1},m_{2})=1 such that π1​(ℙ2∖D)≅𝔽r∗ℤm1∗ℤm2\pi_{1}(\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus D)\cong\mathbb{F}_{r}*\mathbb{Z}_{m_{1}}*\mathbb{Z}_{m_{2}}. Moreover, there exists F=[fqp:fpq]:U=ℙ2∖ℬ→ℙ1F=[f_{q}^{p}:f_{p}^{q}]:U=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}\to\mathbb{P}^{1} an admissible map as in Condition 2.3 such that:

  1. (i)

    FF induces an orbifold morphism

    F|:ℙ2∖D→ℙ(r+1,m¯)1,F_{|}:\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus D\to\mathbb{P}^{1}_{(r+1,\bar{m})},

    where ℙ(r+1,m¯)1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{(r+1,\bar{m})} is maximal with respect to F|F_{|}, and m¯\bar{m} takes the following value: (m1,m2)(m_{1},m_{2}) if m2≥2m_{2}\geq 2, (m1)(m_{1}) if m1≥2m_{1}\geq 2 and m2=1m_{2}=1, and it is empty if m1=m2=1m_{1}=m_{2}=1.

  2. (ii)

    F∗:π1​(ℙ2∖D)→π1orb​(ℙ(r+1,m¯)1)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus D)\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{(r+1,\bar{m})}) is an isomorphism.

  3. (iii)

    D=F−1​(Σ0)¯⊂ℙ2D=\overline{F^{-1}(\Sigma_{0})}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} is a fiber-type curve which is the closure of the union of r+1r+1 irreducible fibers of FF.

More concretely,

  1. (1)

    If m1>m2>1m_{1}>m_{2}>1, then p=m1p=m_{1}, q=m2q=m_{2} and the pencil F=[fm2m1:fm1m2]F=[f_{m_{2}}^{m_{1}}:f_{m_{1}}^{m_{2}}] has exactly two multiple fibers corresponding to [0:1],[1:0]∉Σ0[0:1],[1:0]\notin\Sigma_{0}.

  2. (2)

    If m1>m2=1m_{1}>m_{2}=1, then p=m1p=m_{1}, [1:0]∈Σ0[1:0]\in\Sigma_{0}, and the pencil F=[fqm1:fm1q]F=[f_{q}^{m_{1}}:f_{m_{1}}^{q}] has at least one multiple fiber corresponding to [0:1]∉Σ0[0:1]\notin\Sigma_{0}.

  3. (3)

    If m1=m2=1m_{1}=m_{2}=1, then F=[fqp:fpq]F=[f_{q}^{p}:f_{p}^{q}] has at most two multiple fibers corresponding to [0:1],[1:0]∈Σ0[0:1],[1:0]\in\Sigma_{0}.

Remark 2.15.

This result implies that, if an affine curve satisfies that the fundamental group of its complement in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} is a free product of cyclic groups, then it is a free group, and moreover, the affine curve must consist of a finite union of irreducible fibers of a polynomial map f:ℂ2→ℂf:\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}.

The goal of Section 4 is to find Zariski pairs in this setting, where the irreducible components of both curves will be closures of fibers of the same admissible map.

We introduce the following notation.

Notation 2.16.

Let UU be a smooth quasi-projective surface and let SS be a smooth projective curve. If F:U→SF:U\to S is an admissible map and B⊂SB\subset S is a finite set, we let UBU_{B} be

UB=U∖F−1​(B).U_{B}=U\setminus F^{-1}(B).
Remark 2.17.

Let F=[f:g]:U=ℙ2∖ℬ→ℙ1F=[f:g]:U=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}\to\mathbb{P}^{1} be an admissible map, where f,g∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]f,g\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] are homogeneous polynomials of degree d≥1d\geq 1 with no non-constant common factors, and ℬ=V⁡(f)∩V⁡(g)\mathcal{B}=V(f)\cap V(g). Let BB be a non-empty finite subset of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, and let D=F−1​(B)¯D=\overline{F^{-1}(B)}. Then UB=ℙ2∖DU_{B}=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus D.

The following result can be found in [ji-Eva-orbifold, Thm. 1.4, Cor. 4.9].

Theorem 2.18 (Addition-Deletion Lemma).

Let UU be a smooth quasi-projective surface and let F:U→SF:U\rightarrow S be an admissible map to a smooth projective curve SS. Assume B⊂SB\subset S, where #​B=n≥1\#B=n\geq 1, and let P∈S∖(BF∪B)P\in S\setminus\left(B_{F}\cup B\right), where BFB_{F} is the (finite) set of atypical values of FF.

Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    F∗:π1​(UB)→π1orb​(S∖B)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{B})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus B) is an isomorphism,

  2. (2)

    F∗:π1​(UB∪{P})→π1orb​(S∖(B∪{P}))F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{B\cup\{P\}})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}\left(S\setminus(B\cup\{P\})\right) is an isomorphism,

and in that case,

π1​(UB∪{P})≅ℤ∗π1​(UB).\pi_{1}(U_{B\cup\{P\}})\cong\mathbb{Z}*\pi_{1}(U_{B}).

Moreover, the implication (2)⇒\Rightarrow(1) also holds if P∈BF∖BP\in B_{F}\setminus B.

Remark 2.19.

We will refer to (1)⇒\Rightarrow(2) as the Addition Lemma (which is true for generic fibers) and to (2)⇒\Rightarrow(1) as the Deletion Lemma (which is true for all fibers).

3. Threshold of atypical values

Let UU be a smooth quasi-projective surface and let SS be a smooth projective curve. Let F:U→SF:U\to S be an admissible map and let B⊂SB\subset S be a finite set of points. The goal of this section is to study how the presence of atypical values of FF in BB relates to the induced morphism F∗:π1​(UB)→π1orb​(S∖B)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{B})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus B) being an isomorphism.

To study this problem, we start by defining the set

𝒯F:={T⊂BF|F∗:π1​(U{P}∪T)→π1orb​(S∖({P}∪T)) is an isomorphism},{\mathcal{T}}_{F}:=\left\{T\subset B_{F}\left|\begin{array}[]{c}F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{\{P\}\cup T})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}\left(S\setminus(\{P\}\cup T)\right)\\ \textrm{ is an isomorphism}\end{array}\right.\right\},

where P∈S∖BFP\in S\setminus B_{F}. The following result summarizes some of the properties of 𝒯F{\mathcal{T}}_{F}.

Lemma 3.1.

Let UU be a smooth quasi-projective surface and let SS be a smooth projective curve. Let F:U→SF:U\to S be an admissible map, let BF⊂SB_{F}\subset S be its set of atypical values, and let P∈S∖BFP\in S\setminus B_{F}. The following hold:

  1. (1)

    The set 𝒯F{\mathcal{T}}_{F} is independent of the choice of P∈S∖BFP\in S\setminus B_{F}.

  2. (2)

    If T∈𝒯FT\in{\mathcal{T}}_{F} and T′T^{\prime} is such that T′⊂T⊂BFT^{\prime}\subset T\subset B_{F}, then T′∈𝒯FT^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{T}}_{F}.

  3. (3)

    𝒯F≠∅{\mathcal{T}}_{F}\neq\emptyset if and only if F∗:π1​(UP)→π1orb​(S∖{P})F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{P})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus\{P\}) is an isomorphism.

Proof.

Let P,Q∈S∖BFP,Q\in S\setminus B_{F}, let T⊂BFT\subset B_{F} and suppose that T∈𝒯FT\in{\mathcal{T}}_{F}, that is,

F∗:π1​(U{P}∪T)→π1orb​(S∖({P}∪T))is an isomorphism.F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{\{P\}\cup T})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}\left(S\setminus(\{P\}\cup T)\right)\quad\text{is an isomorphism.}

By the Addition Lemma (Theorem 2.18), one can add the generic fiber of FF at QQ, that is, F∗:π1​(U{P,Q}∪T)→π1orb​(S∖{P,Q}∪T)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{\{P,Q\}\cup T})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus\{P,Q\}\cup T) is an isomorphism. Using now the Deletion Lemma, the fiber at PP can be removed and F∗:π1​(U{Q}∪T)→π1orb​(S∖{Q}∪T)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{\{Q\}\cup T})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus\{Q\}\cup T) is an isomorphism. This proves part (1). Part (2) follows directly from the Deletion Lemma. Part (2) implies that 𝒯F≠∅{\mathcal{T}}_{F}\neq\emptyset if and only if ∅∈𝒯F\emptyset\in{\mathcal{T}}_{F}, which implies part (3). ∎

The previous result suggests the following definition.

Definition 3.2.

Let UU be a smooth quasi-projective surface, let SS be a smooth projective curve. Let F:U→SF:U\to S be an admissible map and let BF⊂SB_{F}\subset S be its set of atypical values. We say that a set T⊂BFT\subset B_{F} is a threshold set of (atypical) values for FF if it is a maximal set of 𝒯F{\mathcal{T}}_{F} (with respect to the inclusion of sets).

Remark 3.3 (Non-empty 𝒯F{\mathcal{T}}_{F}, projective case).

Let F=[fqp:fpq]:U=ℙ2∖ℬ→ℙ1F=[f_{q}^{p}:f_{p}^{q}]:U=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}\to\mathbb{P}^{1} be an admissible map satisfying Condition 2.3. If P∈ℙ1∖BFP\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus B_{F}, then F∗:π1​(UP)→π1orb​(S∖{P})F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{P})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}\left(S\setminus\{P\}\right) is an isomorphism by [ji-Eva-orbifold, Theorem 1.2], hence, Lemma 3.1(3) implies 𝒯F≠∅{\mathcal{T}}_{F}\neq\emptyset.

Example 3.4 (Empty 𝒯F{\mathcal{T}}_{F}).

Consider ℬ=V⁡(h2)∩V⁡(h4)\mathcal{B}=V(h_{2})\cap V(h_{4}), where hdh_{d} is an irreducible homogeneous polynomial in ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] of degree dd for d=2,4d=2,4. Define U=ℙ2∖ℬU=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}, S=ℙ1S=\mathbb{P}^{1}, and F:U→SF:U\to S is described as F=[h22:h4]F=[h_{2}^{2}:h_{4}]. By Lemma 2.6, FF is an admissible map, however F∗:G1:=π1​(UP)→π1orb​(S∖{P})=:G2F_{*}:G_{1}:=\pi_{1}(U_{P})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus\{P\})=:G_{2} is not an isomorphism for any P∉BFP\notin B_{F}, since the abelianizations G1/G1′=ℤ4G_{1}/G^{\prime}_{1}=\mathbb{Z}_{4}, G2/G2′=ℤ2G_{2}/G^{\prime}_{2}=\mathbb{Z}_{2} are not isomorphic. Hence, Lemma 3.1(3) implies 𝒯F=∅{\mathcal{T}}_{F}=\emptyset.

The purpose of 𝒯F{\mathcal{T}}_{F} is to characterize the property that F∗:π1​(UB)→π1orb​(S∖B)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{B})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus B) defines an isomorphism, regardless of whether or not BB contains a generic fiber, as the following result shows.

Proposition 3.5.

Let UU be a smooth quasi-projective surface, SS a smooth projective curve and F:U→SF:U\to S be an admissible map. Consider B⊂SB\subset S a finite non-empty set. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    F∗:π1​(UB)→π1orb​(S∖B)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{B})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus B) is an isomorphism.

  2. (2)

    There exists T∈𝒯FT\in{\mathcal{T}}_{F} such that B∩BF⊂TB\cap B_{F}\subset T.

  3. (3)

    B∩BF∈𝒯FB\cap B_{F}\in{\mathcal{T}}_{F}.

Proof.

Note that (2) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (3) follows immediately from Lemma 3.1(2).

To show (1) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (3) note that the Addition-Deletion Lemma (Theorem 2.18) implies that

F∗:π1​(UB)→π1orb​(S∖B)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{B})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(S\setminus B)

is an isomorphism if and only if

F∗:π1​(U(B∩BF)∪{P})→π1orb​(S∖((B∩BF)∪{P}))F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{(B\cap B_{F})\cup\{P\}})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}\left(S\setminus\left((B\cap B_{F})\cup\{P\}\right)\right)

is an isomorphism for any P∈S∖(BF∪B)P\in S\setminus(B_{F}\cup B), which is true iff B∩BF∈𝒯FB\cap B_{F}\in{\mathcal{T}}_{F}. ∎

In this paper, we will compute the threshold sets of atypical values in cases which fall under the realm of Remark 3.3. In these cases, the threshold sets of atypical values contain more information about the fundamental groups of the complements of the fiber-type curves that arise from FF than the definition of a threshold set of atypical values may suggest, as exemplified by the following result, which may be used in combination with Proposition 3.5.

Proposition 3.6.

Let F=[f:g]:U=ℙ2∖ℬ→ℙ1F=[f:g]:U=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}\to\mathbb{P}^{1} be an admissible map, where f,g∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]f,g\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] are homogeneous polynomials of degree d≥1d\geq 1 with no non-constant common factors, and ℬ=V⁡(f)∩V⁡(g)\mathcal{B}=V(f)\cap V(g). Let B⊂ℙ1B\subset\mathbb{P}^{1} be such that #​B≥2\#B\geq 2. Then, the following are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    π1​(UB)\pi_{1}(U_{B}) is a free product of cyclic groups.

  2. (2)

    FF satisfies (i)–(iii) of Theorem 2.14, so in particular,

    F∗:π1​(UB)=π1​(ℙ2∖F−1​(B)¯)→π1orb​(ℙ1∖B)is an isomorphism.F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{B})=\pi_{1}\left(\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\overline{F^{-1}(B)}\right)\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus B)\quad\text{is an isomorphism.}

    Moreover, possibly after a change of coordinates in ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, FF also satisfies Condition 2.3.

Proof.

The implication (2) ⇒\Rightarrow (1) is trivial. Let us now see the implication (1) ⇒\Rightarrow (2) if #​B≥2\#B\geq 2. Assume that π1​(UB)\pi_{1}(U_{B}) is a free product of cyclic groups. By Theorem 2.14 there exists a pencil G=[guv:gvu]G=[g_{u}^{v}:g_{v}^{u}] satisfying Condition 2.3 and (i)–(iii) of Theorem 2.14. In particular, every curve of the form F−1​(P)¯⊂ℙ2\overline{F^{-1}(P)}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} for P∈BP\in B is the union of the closure of finitely many irreducible fibers of GG. Let [α1:β1],[α2:β2][\alpha_{1}:\beta_{1}],[\alpha_{2}:\beta_{2}] be distinct points in BB. Then,

β1​f−α1​g\displaystyle\beta_{1}f-\alpha_{1}g =guk1​gvk2​∏i=1k3(bi​guv−ai​gvu)li,\displaystyle=g_{u}^{k_{1}}g_{v}^{k_{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{k_{3}}(b_{i}g_{u}^{v}-a_{i}g_{v}^{u})^{l_{i}},
β2​f−α2​g\displaystyle\beta_{2}f-\alpha_{2}g =guk4​gvk5​∏j=1k6(dj​guv−cj​gvu)mj,\displaystyle=g_{u}^{k_{4}}g_{v}^{k_{5}}\prod_{j=1}^{k_{6}}(d_{j}g_{u}^{v}-c_{j}g_{v}^{u})^{m_{j}},

for some kj∈ℤ≥0k_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, j=1,…,6j=1,\ldots,6 with k1+k2+k3≥1k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}\geq 1, k4+k5+k6≥1k_{4}+k_{5}+k_{6}\geq 1, li∈ℤ≥1l_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} for all i=1,…,k3i=1,\ldots,k_{3}, mj∈ℤ≥1m_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} for all j=1,…,k6j=1,\ldots,k_{6}, and [ai:bi],[cj:dj][a_{i}:b_{i}],[c_{j}:d_{j}] distinct points in ℙ1∖{[1:0],[0:1]}\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{[1:0],[0:1]\} for i=1,…,k3i=1,\ldots,k_{3} and j=1,…,k6j=1,\ldots,k_{6}.

Note that, since GG satisfies (iii) of Theorem 2.14 and Condition 2.3, bi​guv−ai​gvub_{i}g_{u}^{v}-a_{i}g_{v}^{u} and dj​guv−cj​gvud_{j}g_{u}^{v}-c_{j}g_{v}^{u} are irreducible polynomials for all i=1,…,k3i=1,\ldots,k_{3} and for all j=1,…,k6j=1,\ldots,k_{6}. Looking at the degrees of the homogeneous polynomials in the previous two equations, we obtain that

d=k1​u+k2​v+u​v​∑i=1k3li=k4​u+k5​v+u​v​∑j=1k6mi.d=k_{1}u+k_{2}v+uv\sum_{i=1}^{k_{3}}l_{i}=k_{4}u+k_{5}v+uv\sum_{j=1}^{k_{6}}m_{i}.

Since uu and vv are coprime, the last equality implies that v|(k1−k4)v\mid(k_{1}-k_{4}) and u|(k2−k5)u\mid(k_{2}-k_{5}). Note that, since different fibers of FF do not have any irreducible components in common, at least one element of the sets {k1,k4}\{k_{1},k_{4}\} and {k2,k5}\{k_{2},k_{5}\} is 00, so v|k1,k4v\mid k_{1},k_{4} and v|k2,k5v\mid k_{2},k_{5}. Hence, there exist homogeneous polynomials h1,h2∈ℂ⁡[x,y]h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] of the same degree d′d^{\prime} such that f=h1​(guv,gvu)f=h_{1}(g_{u}^{v},g_{v}^{u}) and g=h2​(guv,gvu)g=h_{2}(g_{u}^{v},g_{v}^{u}). In other words, FF factors as the composition of GG and [h1:h2]:ℙ1→ℙ1[h_{1}:h_{2}]:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}. Since FF is admissible, then d′=1d^{\prime}=1, and hence [h1:h2][h_{1}:h_{2}] is a change of coordinates in ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. In particular, FF satisfies Condition 2.3 (after possibly a change of coordinates in ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}), and also (i)–(iii) of Theorem 2.14, including the fact that

F∗:π1​(UB)→π1orb​(ℙ1∖B)F_{*}:\pi_{1}(U_{B})\to\pi_{1}^{\orb}(\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus B)

is an isomorphism. ∎

In other words, Propositions 3.5 and 3.6 show that finding all the threshold sets of atypical values for an admissible map FF amounts to completely characterizing when the fundamental group of UB=ℙ2∖F−1​(B)¯U_{B}=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\overline{F^{-1}(B)} is a free product of cyclic groups for all finite B⊂ℙ1B\subset\mathbb{P}^{1} such that #​B≥2\#B\geq 2.

Remark 3.7.

If #​B=1\#B=1 and B⊂ℙ2∖BFB\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus B_{F}, the result of Proposition 3.6 holds by [ji-Eva-orbifold, Theorem 1.2].

However, if #​B=1\#B=1 and B⊂BFB\subset B_{F}, the result is no longer true:

Example 3.8.

Let f2,f3∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]f_{2},f_{3}\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] be irreducible homogeneous polynomials of degrees 22 and 33 respectively. By Lemma 2.6, [f23:f32][f_{2}^{3}:f_{3}^{2}] restricted to its maximal domain of definition is an admissible map. 4. Zariski pairs of fiber-type curves

Consider F:ℙ2⇢ℙ1F:\mathbb{P}^{2}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} the rational morphism defined as [f¯(x,y,z):z6][\bar{f}(x,y,z):z^{6}], where f⁡(x,y)=x6+y6+6​x​yf(x,y)=x^{6}+y^{6}+6xy and f¯​(x,y,z)=x6+y6+6​x​y​z4\bar{f}(x,y,z)=x^{6}+y^{6}+6xyz^{4}. This rational map is not well defined on the base points ℬ={[x:y:0]∈ℙ2∣x6+y6=0}\mathcal{B}=\{[x:y:0]\in\mathbb{P}^{2}\mid x^{6}+y^{6}=0\}. The generic fiber of the resulting admissible map F:U→ℙ1F:U\to\mathbb{P}^{1}, where U=ℙ2∖ℬU=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus\mathcal{B}, is a smooth sextic (with six points removed). The set of atypical values of FF is BF={0,∞,±4,±4​i}⊂ℙ1≡ℂ∪{∞}B_{F}=\{0,\infty,\pm 4,\pm 4i\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{1}\equiv\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}. The fiber F−1​(∞)F^{-1}(\infty) is the only multiple fiber and it has multiplicity six. The fiber F−1​(0)F^{-1}(0) is a singular sextic with one node. The remaining atypical fibers are irreducible sextics with six nodes. In particular, FF is an admissible map satisfying Condition 2.3. For any finite set B⊂ℙ1B\subset\mathbb{P}^{1} we will denote CB:=F−1​(B)¯C_{B}:=\overline{F^{-1}(B)}. The purpose of this section is to study π1​(UB)\pi_{1}(U_{B}) for UB:=ℙ2∖CBU_{B}:=\mathbb{P}^{2}\setminus C_{B} for different choices of BB. In particular, we will exhibit a Zariski pair of affine nodal curves and another Zariski pair of projective sextics of fiber-type.

4.2. A projective Zariski pair

In this section we continue using the notation presented at the beginning of §4. One can obtain a Zariski pair of projective curves in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} as follows.

The projective curves (C{4,−4},C{4,4​i})(C_{\{4,-4\}},C_{\{4,4i\}}) form a Zariski pair of projective curves of degree 12 whose complements in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} have non-isomorphic fundamental groups. More concretely, π1​(U{4,4​i})=ℤ∗ℤ6\pi_{1}(U_{\{4,4i\}})=\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}_{6}, whereas

Remark 4.7.

As seen in the proof of Lemma , the three lines containing the 12 nodes in C{4,−4}C_{\{4,-4\}} are the preimages of ℓ1={v=0}\ell_{1}=\{v=0\} and ℓ+={v=3u}\ell_{+}=\{v=3u\}. The latter passes through the nodes (±1,±3)(\pm 1,\pm 3) and it intersects the two cubics H±4H_{\pm 4} transversally at two other smooth points, namely (∓2,∓6)(\mp 2,\mp 6), and hence the preimage of ℓ+\ell_{+} by δ∘σ\delta\circ\sigma (which splits in two lines 6​x+(5+11​i)​y=06x+(5+\sqrt{11}i)y=0 and 6​x+(5−11​i)​y=06x+(5-\sqrt{11}i)y=0) contains 8 nodes (4 each line) and it intersects C{4,−4}C_{\{4,-4\}} transversally at the remaining 8 points of intersection (again, 4 each line). On the other hand, ℓ1\ell_{1} is tangent to the two cubics at (±1,0)(\pm 1,0) and it intersects them transversally at two other points (∓2,0)(\mp 2,0). This implies that its preimage (a ramification line x+y=0x+y=0) passes through 4 nodes (the preimage of a simple tangency to a ramification locus of order two becomes two nodes) and through 4 additional transversal intersections (the preimages of (±2,0)(\pm 2,0)). In particular, the three lines passing through the 12 nodes are concurrent and the remaining intersection points of any of these three lines with the curve C{4,−4}C_{\{4,-4\}} are transversal intersections (4 transversal intersections per line). This stresses the fact that the only difference between the position of the singularities of the curves (C{4,−4},C{4,4​i})(C_{\{4,-4\}},C_{\{4,4i\}}) is the contribution of the special position of the nodes, and the same goes for (CB1=C{4,−4,∞},CB2=C{4,4​i,∞})(C_{B_{1}}=C_{\{4,-4,\infty\}},C_{B_{2}}=C_{\{4,4i,\infty\}}) (that is, the projective curves whose complements in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} are ℂ2∖D1\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus D_{1} and ℂ2∖D2\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus D_{2} respectively).

5. Twisted Alexander polynomials for SU⁡(2)\SU(2)-representations

The purpose of this section is to show that twisted Alexander polynomials can also distinguish the fundamental groups G1=π1​(UB1)G_{1}=\pi_{1}(U_{B_{1}}) and G2=π1​(UB2)G_{2}=\pi_{1}(U_{B_{2}}) presented in 4.1. To our knowledge, this is the first example in the literature of a Zariski pair whose groups have the same Alexander invariant but different twisted Alexander polynomials. Moreover, Lemma  shows that the position of the nodes affects the fundamental groups and twisted Alexander polynomials are sensitive to this special position. Classical Alexander polynomials and characteristic varieties are known not to be sensitive to the position of nodes (see for instance [Libgober-Alexander-invariants] and [Libgober-characteristic, 2.5]). We refer the reader to [CF, Section 2] for a quick introduction on twisted Alexander polynomials and how to compute them.

We first compute the Alexander invariant of the complements UB1U_{B_{1}} and UB2U_{B_{2}}.

Proposition 5.1.

The Alexander invariant of both ℂ2∖D1\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus D_{1} and ℂ2∖D2\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus D_{2} is ℂ⁡[t1±1,t2±1]\mathbb{C}[t_{1}^{\pm 1},t_{2}^{\pm 1}].

Proof.

Let us denote by MjM_{j} the Alexander invariant of ℂ2∖Dj\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus D_{j}, that is, Mj:=Gj′/Gj′′M_{j}:=G^{\prime}_{j}/G^{\prime\prime}_{j} as an RR-module where R=ℂ⁡[Gj/Gj′]=ℂ⁡[t1±1,t2±1]R=\mathbb{C}[G_{j}/G^{\prime}_{j}]=\mathbb{C}[t_{1}^{\pm 1},t_{2}^{\pm 1}]. It is immediate that M2=[x,y]​RM_{2}=[x,y]R. As for M1M_{1}, one can use the presentation (2), where the abelian classes of xx and yy generate G1/G1′G_{1}/G^{\prime}_{1} and u,v∈G1′u,v\in G^{\prime}_{1}. Using [Artal-ji-Tokunaga-survey-zariski, §2.5], this implies that M1M_{1} is generated by [x,y][x,y], uu, and vv and whose relations are given by rewriting the relations in (3) as elements of the RR-module M1M_{1}. Since [x,q]=0[x,q]=0 in M1M_{1} as long as q∈G1′q\in G^{\prime}_{1}, the first two relations in (3) become trivial and the last ones become u=v=0u=v=0. This shows M1≅M2≅RM_{1}\cong M_{2}\cong R. ∎

By Proposition 5.1, the characteristic varieties of UB1U_{B_{1}} and UB2U_{B_{2}} are both (ℂ∗)2(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2}. Analogously, the Alexander polynomials associated with any homomorphism ε:Gj→ℤ2\varepsilon:G_{j}\to\mathbb{Z}^{2} are trivial.

In light of Lemma , this is the announced result showing that twisted Alexander polynomials (associated with non-abelian representations) can be sensitive to the position of nodes.

It is also worth noting that the representation ρ 1 factors though one of the degree-two representations of the binary octahedral group BO 48 . The group BO 48 is the finite group of symmetries of the octahedron and it is a non-abelian solvable subgroup of order 48 of SU ( 2 ) .
